title: Measuring Non-Stabilizerness in an SU(2) Lattice Gauge Theory
abstract: One of the goals of quantum simulation is to provide novel insights into quantum systems, such as the gauge theories that are relevant for high-energy and nuclear physics. Recent years have seen rapid improvements in both the hardware and software necessary for these simulations. A central consideration in the design of such simulations is the quantum complexity of a given quantum state. This work takes a step towards studying a specific kind of complexity, namely the non-stabilizerness, in a simple yet non-trivial system: SU(2) lattice gauge theory of two plaquettes. The non-stabilizerness of low-energy eigenstates is studied and the implications for quantum simulations are discussed. The real-time evolution of this system is simulated on ibm_marrakesh and the non-stabilizerness is measured using a random measurement protocol. New techniques enhancing the efficiency of this protocol are developed, including both a new way to calculate the estimator for non-stabilizerness and a flexible error mitigation technique called Bit String Decoherence Renormalization. This mitigation method is central to accurately resolving the experimental time dependence of non-stabilizerness, and is anticipated to have broad applicability in digital quantum simulations.
summary: This work develops methods to measure non-stabilizerness—a measure of quantum complexity—in SU(2) Lattice Gauge Theory simulations. It addresses hardware limitations by introducing Bit String Decoherence Renormalization (BSDR) and utilizing advanced estimators based on the Walsh-Hadamard transform. The results demonstrate how complex physical properties can be extracted from noisy quantum measurements.
main_problem: The study quantifies quantum complexity, specifically non-stabilizerness, for simulating lattice gauge theories on near-term quantum hardware.
main_result: Non-stabilizerness is shown to be a measurable quantity that exhibits predictable convergence behavior with increasing digitization resolution and can be accurately estimated using advanced error mitigation techniques like BSDR.
method: The work employs randomized measurement protocols, novel estimators derived via the Walsh-Hadamard transform, and the Bit String Decoherence Renormalization (BSDR) technique to mitigate noise effects on bitstring probability distributions.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is SU(2) Lattice Gauge Theory restricted to two plaquettes. The simulation involves mapping the continuous gauge field Hilbert space onto a finite qudit register via digitization and studying low-energy eigenstates.
key_observables: Non-stabilizerness ($M_2$ or $S_2$), Stabilizer Rényi Entropy, Total Variational Distance (TVD), and bitstring probability distributions $p(s)$.
important_parameters: Gauge coupling constant ($g$), digitization resolution ($n_q$), and the error mitigation parameters ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that low-energy wavefunctions can be approximated by smooth functions, allowing for efficient reconstruction of probability distributions using Walsh coefficients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup (gauge fixing/digitization), the dependence of non-stabilizerness on gauge coupling and resolution, and diagrams detailing the structure of the Walsh hierarchy used for error mitigation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and complexity measure to developing advanced measurement protocols (WH transform estimators) and finally introducing novel error mitigation techniques (BSDR) validated against theoretical bounds (TVD).
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, quantifiable metric (non-stabilizerness) for assessing the feasibility of simulating complex quantum field theories on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
